title: Minimum Value to Get Positive Step by Step Sum
description: Find the minimum positive startValue by simulating candidates one at a time in brute force, then optimize to a single pass that tracks the running sum and its minimum.

sections.title: Minimum Value to Get Positive Step by Step Sum

content.title: Minimum Value to Get Positive Step by Step Sum

blocks.text: You are given an array of integers nums and you begin with a positive integer startValue. Walking through nums from left to right, you keep a running total that starts at startValue and add each element to it in turn. This running total is called the step by step sum. Your task is to find the smallest positive startValue such that this step by step sum never drops below 1 at any point during the scan.

blocks.caption: Scan nums once, track the running sum and its minimum, then recover startValue

blocks.text: Restated simply: nums describes a sequence of changes applied one after another to a running total that begins at startValue. After every single change, that running total must still be at least 1. We are free to choose startValue, and we want the smallest positive number that makes this true for the whole array.

blocks.title: Think of it as a bank balance
blocks.text: Imagine nums as a sequence of daily transactions on a bank account, deposits and withdrawals applied from left to right. startValue is the opening balance you choose to deposit before day one. The bank rule is simple: the balance can never drop to zero or below on any day. To find the smallest safe opening balance, you only need to know how low the balance would have gone if you had opened the account with 0, then add just enough cushion so that worst day still reads 1.

blocks.caption: The lowest point the balance would reach sets the exact cushion needed

blocks.text: The minimum running sum, including the initial 0 before any element, is -4. So startValue = 1 - (-4) = 5, which matches the expected output.

blocks.text: The minimum running sum, including the initial 0, never leaves 0 because nums never pulls it negative. So startValue = 1 - 0 = 1, confirming that whenever nums never dips into negative territory, the answer is simply the smallest positive integer, 1.

Before jumping to code, it helps to separate the two things being added together at every step: the fixed shape of nums, and the constant startValue we are trying to choose. That separation is the entire key to this problem.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If we just simulate the step by step sum starting from a guessed startValue, we would guess a number, run through the whole array, check whether it ever drops below 1, and if it does, increase the guess and repeat the whole scan again. That is a lot of repeated work for a question that should have one direct answer.

Observation 2: Notice that startValue is added to the same running sum at every single step. So the step by step sum at step i is always startValue plus the plain sum of the first i elements of nums. The only thing that changes across steps is that plain prefix sum, never startValue itself.

Observation 3: Since startValue is a constant added everywhere, the step by step sum is smallest exactly where the plain prefix sum of nums alone, starting from 0, is smallest. Find that one minimum prefix sum value in a single left to right scan, and the worst case for the entire array has been captured.

Observation 4: Once the lowest point the plain prefix sum reaches is known, call it minPrefix, we need startValue + minPrefix to be at least 1. Solving for startValue gives startValue = 1 - minPrefix directly, with no repeated guessing required. The whole simulate and check loop collapses into one pass that tracks a running sum and its running minimum.

This is the same shift in thinking that shows up across the prefix sum pattern: instead of repeating a scan for every candidate answer, scan once, record the one summary value that matters, then compute the answer from it directly.

A direct way to solve this is to try candidate values of startValue one at a time, starting from 1, and for each candidate simulate the entire step by step sum across nums. If the running total ever drops below 1 for a candidate, that candidate fails and the search moves to the next larger one. The first candidate for which the running total stays at least 1 the whole way through is the answer.

items: Start testing candidate = 1.
For the current candidate, set running = candidate.
Scan nums from left to right, adding each element to running.
If running ever drops below 1 during the scan, this candidate fails, so increase candidate by 1 and restart the scan from the beginning.
If the scan completes without running ever dropping below 1, return the current candidate as the answer.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The candidate is increased one at a time and the simulation restarted completely, because a smaller candidate that fails only tells us it is not enough, not exactly how much more is needed.
Breaking out of the inner loop the moment running drops below 1 avoids wasting time simulating the rest of a candidate that has already failed.
The search starts at candidate = 1 because the problem requires startValue to be a positive integer.

blocks.text: This brute force approach is easy to reason about because it mirrors the problem statement directly: pick a number, check it against the whole array, try the next one if it fails. But that direct simulation is exactly what makes it slow.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time complexity is O(n times answer) in the worst case, since the simulation may be retried once for every candidate value from 1 up to the final answer, and each simulation scans all n elements of nums. Space complexity is O(1) beyond the input array, since only a running total is tracked at a time.

When nums contains a large negative dip, the correct startValue can itself be large, and repeating a full scan of nums for every candidate from 1 up to that value wastes enormous effort recomputing the same running sums again and again.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
The brute force wastes effort because it recomputes the entire running sum from scratch for every single candidate, even though the shape of that running sum never actually changes, only the constant startValue added on top of it does.

The key insight is to separate the two things being added together: the fixed contribution of nums, and the variable contribution of startValue. Scanning nums exactly once, using a running sum that starts at 0 instead of startValue, reveals the single lowest point that sum ever reaches. Call it minPrefix.

Because every step by step sum is just startValue plus that step's plain prefix sum of nums, the entire array can never violate the at least 1 rule as long as startValue + minPrefix is at least 1. That is one inequality, solved once, instead of an entire family of repeated simulations.
This turns an O(n times answer) search into a single O(n) pass followed by one arithmetic step, because the only information that ever mattered from the whole array was its single worst prefix sum.

Scan nums once while keeping two running values: runningSum, the plain prefix sum of nums starting from 0, and minPrefix, the smallest value runningSum has taken so far, including the initial 0 before any element is added. After the scan, the answer is 1 - minPrefix.

codes.python:
def min_start_value(nums):
    running_sum = 0
    min_prefix = 0
    for x in nums:
        running_sum += x
        min_prefix = min(min_prefix, running_sum)
    return 1 - min_prefix


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [-3, 2, -3, 4, 2]
    result = min_start_value(nums)
    print(result)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time complexity is O(n), a single left to right pass over nums. Space complexity is O(1), just two integer variables regardless of input size.

The step by step sum at any point is always startValue plus the plain prefix sum of nums up to that point, so the entire array satisfies the at least 1 rule exactly when startValue is large enough to cover the single worst (lowest) prefix sum, minPrefix. Solving startValue + minPrefix >= 1 for the smallest positive integer gives startValue = 1 - minPrefix. Since minPrefix is always at most 0 (it starts at 0), this value is guaranteed to be at least 1.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens"],"rows":[["minPrefix = 0 (nums never dips below its starting value)","startValue = 1 - 0 = 1, the smallest possible positive value"],["minPrefix is negative","startValue = 1 - minPrefix, exactly enough to cushion the lowest dip"],["minPrefix is very negative (a large dip)","startValue grows correspondingly larger to compensate"]]}

items: runningSum starts at 0 and accumulates nums exactly like the step by step sum would, minus the startValue term.
minPrefix tracks the smallest value runningSum has taken at any point using a single comparison per element.
The final answer, 1 - minPrefix, is computed once after the loop finishes, with no retrying or re-scanning.

blocks.text: This problem is a clean example of the prefix sum pattern: instead of tracking the whole array at every candidate, track one running total and one running summary value, then solve the rest with simple arithmetic.

items: Forgetting to include the initial value of 0 in the minimum, which causes an error when nums never goes negative (the answer must still be exactly 1, not 0).
Confusing the running sum used to find minPrefix with the actual step by step sum that includes startValue, they are different sums.
Re-simulating with a fresh startValue guess for every candidate instead of realizing one single pass is enough.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["nums contains only positive numbers","minPrefix stays at 0, so the answer is always 1"],["nums is a single very negative element","minPrefix equals that element, so startValue must offset it exactly"],["nums.length == 1","The loop runs once; minPrefix is either 0 or nums[0], whichever is smaller"]]}

items: Say out loud that startValue is a constant added to every prefix, so the whole problem reduces to finding one number, the minimum prefix sum.
Mention the O(n) one-pass solution early rather than describing the brute force in detail, then briefly note why the brute force is slower if asked.
Double check that the initial minPrefix is set to 0, not to nums[0], since the empty prefix before any elements also has to satisfy the constraint.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer asks you to return the smallest value that keeps a running total non-negative or positive throughout a scan, think prefix sum plus running minimum, then solve directly for the missing starting offset instead of simulating candidates.

items: How would your answer change if the running sum needed to stay at least 0 instead of at least 1?
Could you solve this if nums was streamed one element at a time instead of given as a full array upfront?
How would you adapt this approach if you needed the minimum startValue for several different threshold values in one query?
This is a minimum-prefix-sum variant of the same prefix sum family as Find Pivot Index, both track a running total across the array in one pass.
It shares its running total mindset with Find the Highest Altitude, where a running sum of gains and losses is scanned to find an extreme value.
The trick of separating a constant offset from a running total generalizes to many "find the minimum starting condition" style problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The optimized one-pass solution runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, a single scan that tracks a running sum and its minimum, followed by one arithmetic step to recover startValue.

items: Pattern: Prefix sum with a running minimum
Core Idea: startValue is a constant offset added to every prefix sum of nums, so only the single lowest prefix sum matters
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The step by step sum's worst case is always startValue plus the minimum prefix sum of nums alone
Interview Difficulty: Easy to Medium, the trick is recognizing the algebraic reduction rather than the coding itself
One-line memory trick: Find the lowest the plain running sum ever falls, then startValue is just 1 minus that
